coverage.headline: Generative AI – Intellectual Property Cases and Policy Tracker (Elsevier v. Meta Entry)
coverage.summary: Mishcon de Reya's live tracker (updated approximately three weeks before August 15, 2026) records the full procedural timeline of the case through the plaintiffs' July 13 opposition to Meta's venue-transfer motion, confirming the case remains before Judge P. Kevin Castel in the S.D.N.Y. pending his ruling.

coverage.headline: Elsevier Inc. et al v. Meta Platforms, Inc. et al — Case Docket (Venue Transfer Motion)
coverage.summary: Per the live docket, Meta and Zuckerberg filed motions to transfer venue to the Northern District of California on June 26, 2026, per Judge Castel's June 10 order; plaintiffs filed their opposition on July 13, and Meta's reply was due July 20 — with Judge Castel's ruling on the transfer motion still pending as of the latest docket entries.

coverage.headline: Elsevier et al. sue Meta over AI training: what's at stake for researchers?
coverage.summary: UCL's copyright team analyzed the complaint's allegations that Meta downloaded unlawful copies, stripped authorship information, and flooded the market with substitutive outputs including verbatim reproductions and hallucinated distortions of original works, outlining implications for academic authors and scholarly publishing markets.

coverage.headline: Authors Sue Meta's AI Scientists Directly in Llama Copyright Case
coverage.summary: A related proposed class action targets not only Meta and Mark Zuckerberg but the individual research scientists alleged to have carried out the company's mass copying of tens of millions of books for Llama training data, escalating personal liability exposure beyond the corporate defendant.

coverage.headline: Major Publishers Challenge AI Training Practices in Landmark Copyright Suit Against Meta
coverage.summary: Holland & Knight's legal analysis explained how the complaint alleges Meta trained Llama on over 267 terabytes of pirated material, masked its IP addresses during torrenting, and stripped copyright management information — allegations crafted to defeat a fair use defense and establish willfulness for enhanced damages, building on the Bartz v. Anthropic framework.

coverage.headline: As Elsevier sues Meta over AI, other scholarly publishers are keeping a watchful eye
coverage.summary: C&EN reports that while Elsevier has joined the class action against Meta, other scholarly publishers are monitoring the case closely, with some having instead pursued licensing deals with AI companies for training data.

coverage.headline: Elsevier Joins Suit Against Meta Over Use of Copyrighted Research in LLM Training
coverage.summary: R&D World reported that Elsevier's complaint provides specific evidence of Llama reproducing sections of copyrighted academic texts word-for-word, and that Elsevier requests the maximum statutory damages under both the Copyright Act and the DMCA, plus a permanent injunction and destruction of all infringing copies.

coverage.headline: Elsevier vs Meta: first science publisher sues over scraped research papers
coverage.summary: Nature highlighted Elsevier's participation in the class-action suit as a landmark moment, marking the first time a major science publisher has sued an AI company over the alleged reproduction of copyrighted research papers used in model training.

coverage.headline: Publishers and Authors Sue Meta, Alleging 'Massive' Copyright Infringement Behind Its Llama AI Service
coverage.summary: The piece highlights the coordinated litigation strategy behind the Meta suit, noting that two of the publisher plaintiffs — Cengage and Hachette — are simultaneously seeking to intervene as class representatives in In Re Google Generative AI Copyright Litigation over Google's Gemini AI. The complaint alleges Zuckerberg personally directed the decision to pirate rather than license works after licensing talks were escalated to him in April 2023.

coverage.headline: Major publishers sue Meta over Llama AI training on books
coverage.summary: Reporting attributed to the Financial Times described the suit as alleging 'one of the most massive infringements of copyrighted materials in history,' with plaintiffs claiming Meta accessed pirated works from shadow libraries, stripped attribution data, and that Zuckerberg personally authorized the conduct after abandoning licensing talks.

coverage.headline: Meta Hit With New AI Copyright Class Action From Publishers
coverage.summary: Bloomberg Law reported that five major publishers and author Scott Turow filed a proposed class action against Meta in the Southern District of New York (Case No. 1:26-cv-03689), with boutique firm Oppenheim + Zebrak representing plaintiffs. Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

coverage.headline: Book Publishers, Scott Turow Sue Meta Over Llama AI Training on Pirated Works
coverage.summary: Law360 reported that book publishers and legal novelist Scott Turow hit Meta Platforms with a proposed class action in New York federal court, accusing it of training its Llama large language models on millions of copyrighted books and articles sourced from pirate sites rather than licensing the material. The case is assigned to Judge P. Kevin Castel in the Southern District of New York.

coverage.headline: Scott Turow's Latest Real-Life Legal Thriller: Suing Meta for Copyright Infringement
coverage.summary: NPR reported that publishers Hachette, Macmillan, McGraw Hill, Elsevier, and Cengage joined forces with novelist Scott Turow to sue Meta and Zuckerberg, alleging Meta knowingly copied copyrighted materials from pirate sites such as LibGen and Anna's Archive to train Llama — with Zuckerberg's personal authorization. Meta said it plans to 'fight this lawsuit aggressively.'
